# Problem, context and actor language

**Accepted authoring direction for Execution and Operating Model documents**, recorded in the [decision](../../notes/decisions/problem-context-and-actor-language.md). The core requirements below concern how the work is explained. The examples and checks show how to apply that direction.

<a id="core-requirements"></a>

## Core requirements

1. **Establish the subject, context and motivating problem at the start.** Identify the project, arrangement or activity being discussed, the situation in which it matters, and the problem, opportunity or purpose it addresses. The opening must let a reader recognize what this particular document is trying to help with.
2. **Make needs specific enough to interpret.** Identify whose need is being expressed, the situation, and the desired condition or outcome. State the motivating problem, opportunity or purpose with the need or in clearly associated context. Distinguish an observed difficulty from a reported concern, a proposal or a hypothetical example; do not invent a shortfall to make a need sound concrete.
3. **Start participant references with a recognizable category.** Use human and agent in place of personal names, and declare programmatic participants where relevant; see the accepted dot notation below. Add a role qualifier when needed to distinguish participants or explain their involvement, such as human directing the work, human reviewer, authoring agent or reviewing agent. The situation and problem must remain concrete after the name is removed.

These are information requirements, not a mandatory set of headings, document kinds or YAML fields. Use concise prose and clearly linked shared context where it avoids repetition. When a statement is extracted for another reader or agent, include the context needed to interpret it.

<a id="participant-declarations"></a>

## Declare participants and attribute needs

The human [directed this extension](../../notes/decisions/participant-declarations-and-need-attribution.md): near the start of a document, declare the human, agent and relevant programmatic types, roles or groups used in it, with enough context to distinguish them; attribute each need to the relevant participants or groups. Use a shared declaration and references rather than repeating its full explanation.

For this implementation, distinguish kind, role, group and particular participant as explained in [actors and need attribution](../ontology/concepts/actors-and-roles.md#participant-descriptions-and-need-attribution--proposal). State whether roles are held by the same or different participants when that matters, and what is unknown. Preserve who reported or inferred a need separately from whose need it is. A proposed group need does not establish that all group members agree.

Requirements additionally identify their subject, origin and intended contribution. Do not force every requirement to have a previously written operating need: [the origin proposal](../ontology/concepts/requirement.md#requirement-origins-and-contribution--proposal) explains how vision-derived candidates and unresolved links can be recorded honestly. The exact origin vocabulary and [trade-off treatment](../assessment/competing-needs-and-tradeoffs.md) remain proposals.

<a id="category-first-labels"></a>

## Category-first references and programmatic participants

The human [directed that references start with a recognizable participant category and include programmatic consumers](../../notes/decisions/programmatic-participants-and-category-first-labels.md). Use dot-separated references in the form `<category>.<subject>[.<subsubject>...].<role>`: category first, role last, and a subject path with no fixed depth between them. The [accepted depth extension](../../notes/decisions/hierarchical-participant-role-labels.md) allows a system, subsystem and further nested scope, such as `human.system.subsystem.maintainer` or `agent.case.requirements.author`. Brackets and ellipsis describe optional repeated segments; they are not literal label characters. Declare what the path means locally; a nested name does not by itself assert physical composition, inheritance or authority. The human selected dot notation so that the subject and role remain separately visible: `human.standard.maintainer`, `agent.standard.author`, or `human.system.maintainer`. The subject names what the role concerns; it does not identify an assignee or establish ownership. Dot notation is an accepted authoring convention. The third-category term **program** remains a working choice; these local labels are not a registered naming scheme or a settled universal taxonomy.

Examples in the self-application map are `human.standard.maintainer`, `human.standard.user`, `agent.standard.author`, `agent.standard.reviewer` and the prospective `program.standard.validator`. These replace the earlier opaque abbreviations in the current reading view. A label names a role in this context, not a unique individual. Record the actual assignee, responsibility scope and authority separately; a label alone can name an unfilled role and grants no authority. Separate role-to-instance bindings are needed when two individuals fill the same role. Preserve established identity separately when durable references need to survive a label change.

Here, program means participation through a declared programmatic interface. An AI agent is also software; a program can also be modeled as a system. See [programmatic participants](../ontology/concepts/actors-and-roles.md#programmatic-participants--proposal) for overlap and boundary handling. Do not infer capabilities, speed, autonomy, reliability or authority from the prefix. Document the relevant behavior and constraints.

<a id="actor-language"></a>

## Interpreting human and agent

In this document-authoring convention, **human** identifies a human participant and **agent** identifies an AI participant. A role qualifier describes the participant's role in the stated context. It does not assign responsibility, grant authority or establish that the participant performed an action. Use the applicable assignment or decision as the basis for those claims; see [actors and roles](../ontology/concepts/actors-and-roles.md).

The convention concerns participant naming in reusable model prose. Retain project, standard and business names when they identify the subject being discussed; for example, **Execution and Operating Model** still names this standard. Preserve exact quotations, historical records and source attribution rather than rewriting evidence to fit an editorial convention. Those names are not substitutes for explaining the actual problem.

When multiple humans or agents participate, use distinct role descriptions or existing case identifiers, with assignments explicit where they matter. “The human approved it” is insufficient if the case contains two humans with different authority. If a role or assignment is unknown, state that rather than inventing one. These labels do not adopt a new exhaustive taxonomy of actors or change the meanings of agent in external source vocabularies.

## Applying the rule to needs and requirements

A useful need states **who needs what, in which situation, and for what problem, opportunity or purpose**. The motivating context can be adjacent rather than repeated inside a long sentence. A desire to explore or enjoy something can supply the purpose; an already measured failure is not required.

For a requirement, make clear **what it applies to and what condition it calls for**, with its applicable context and intended contribution recoverable from the text or a direct link. The subject may be a standard artifact, system or process; do not replace such a subject with human or agent merely to follow the naming convention. A requirement such as “the standard is to represent contribution rationales” remains about the standard.

This guidance improves how statements are expressed. It does not establish that a stated need is shared by every human, that a requirement is sufficient, or that a named participant has authority. The substantive [need](../ontology/concepts/need.md) and [requirement](../ontology/concepts/requirement.md) questions retain their existing accepted or proposed scope.

<a id="patterns"></a>

## Patterns and anti-patterns

| Wording or situation | Problem with that reading | Better pattern |
| --- | --- | --- |
| “The human needs clarity.” | Neither the activity nor the difficulty is identifiable. | “When a human evaluates a tool or system design for a personal project or business operation, they need to explain which requirements it would meet and why pursuing those requirements is justified for the intended purpose.” Pair this with the motivating concern about premature tool choice. |
| Replacing a personal name with human while leaving the rest generic. | Actor naming alone does not supply context or purpose. | Keep the project or activity, the decision being made, and the desired condition explicit. |
| “Humans cannot coordinate their businesses.” | Turns a concern or possible failure into an unsupported universal claim. | “A documented process can leave responsibilities unclear; the human reviewing that process needs to identify the participants and their assignments.” State whether an actual omission was observed in this case. |
| “The human approved the change” when two humans participate. | Does not identify whose decision mattered or its scope. | Identify the human holding the relevant decision role and the basis of the decision. A role label alone is not proof of authority. |
| “The human needs to explore a subject for enjoyment.” | There may be no prior failure to repair. | State the exploration or enjoyment purpose and relevant context without inventing a problem or numeric target. |
| Applying the naming rule to a quoted source or replacing the name of the standard with agent. | Alters evidence or changes the statement's subject. | Preserve source attribution and the named subject; use human/agent for participants in the authored model prose. |

## Authoring check and worked application

Read the opening and one need without the rest of the conversation. A human or agent should be able to identify the subject, situation, intended beneficiary, desired condition, and motivating problem, opportunity or purpose, including what is observed versus only proposed. If the passage still fits almost any project unchanged, examine whether important context is missing; broad applicability by itself is not a defect.

The [self-application map](../../../source-locators.md#source-dbda9684ccaf624a) is the first worked application. Its named project and contextual needs remain; its participants are expressed through human, agent and prospective program roles. The human's feedback that the revised opening and needs were clearer supports this authoring decision for the current work. It does not establish that every intended reader will interpret the whole standard correctly.
